segments.title: What should the interwar Royal Navy carrier have been?
segments.body: Retaining two Admiral-class hulls would give Britain a plausible starting point for larger interwar carriers. Conversion under the Washington treaty rules could produce ships comparable in broad role to Lexington, Saratoga, Akagi, and Kaga, raising the baseline for aircraft capacity, protection, and fleet speed. The trade would probably cost Courageous and Glorious as operational warships, although disarming them for training remained an option. Furious could remain available under the experimental-carrier provisions. Later reductions would then begin with a more capable carrier force.

evidence.note: The two-hull Admiral conversion proposal, the Washington treaty allowance, and the trade-off involving Courageous, Glorious and Furious.

segments.summary: Drachinifel proposes retaining two Admiral-class battlecruiser hulls to form the Royal Navy's large interwar carrier force.
segments.question: What would the ideal pre-Second World War aircraft carrier have looked like for the Royal Navy?
segments.answerShort: Convert two surviving Admiral-class battlecruiser hulls into large carriers, accepting the loss of Courageous and Glorious to gain a faster, more capable interwar carrier core.

segments.title: Cammell Laird's missing Admiral-class conversion studies
segments.body: Cammell Laird was selected to build Ark Royal as a strike-carrier specialist, although the yard had never previously built an aircraft carrier. Clarke found references to studies for converting its Admiral-class battlecruiser hull during his PhD research, but had not located the studies themselves. The progress of the hull when conversion was considered remains uncertain. He suspects Beatty helped stop the project, while Drachinifel connects that suggestion with Beatty's contemporary proposal to use Eagle for nocturnal torpedo attacks as well as daytime aviation. Eagle's roughly 24-knot speed and limited manoeuvrability make the latter proposal questionable in their assessment.

evidence.note: Clarke's research references to conversion studies, unresolved hull progress, and the criticism of Beatty's proposed night torpedo role for Eagle.

segments.summary: References to Admiral-class conversion studies help explain Cammell Laird's reputation as a strike-carrier specialist before building Ark Royal.

segments.title: How large carriers could have strengthened the Fleet Air Arm
segments.body: Ships carrying prestigious names such as Howe and Rodney would likely have justified an earlier rear admiral responsible for aircraft carriers. A larger naval air establishment would also have made the case for separate Fleet Air Arm aircraft designs and greater control of procurement. Larger decks and aircraft capacity could bring night-strike and long-range-strike concepts forward because the service would have room for the heavier aircraft those missions demanded. With perhaps 300 aircraft at sea and 500 to 600 including training and reserves, naval orders would be large enough to support dedicated fighters and torpedo bombers. The size of the force would strengthen the case for retaining the expertise needed to specify its aircraft.

evidence.note: Prestigious ship names, senior carrier command, larger aircraft orders, and greater Fleet Air Arm influence over procurement.

segments.summary: Large Admiral-class conversions might have raised naval aviation's institutional status and improved the Royal Navy's influence over aircraft requirements.

segments.title: Why naval aero engineers needed direct links with industry
segments.body: Naval aero engineers needed direct contact with aircraft companies to learn what industry could build and translate operational needs into engineering requirements. Retaining pilots alone would not provide that connection. The rear admiral responsible for aircraft carriers consulted Royal Navy observers because the pilots belonged to the RAF. Requirements then passed through the Admiralty and Air Ministry to industry, with technical feedback returning through the same chain. Each translation created another opportunity for error even when the people involved were competent and acting in good faith.

evidence.note: Naval aero engineers' industrial contacts, the observers' role in requirements, and repeated Admiralty-Air Ministry handoffs.

segments.summary: Several naval and Air Ministry offices separated Fleet Air Arm experience from the engineers designing its aircraft.

segments.title: A layered interwar carrier fleet
segments.body: Capability differences would encourage clearer specialization. Furious and Eagle could replenish or support the big carriers, Hermes could continue cruiser-carrier duties on distant stations, and Argus might be sacrificed earlier to treaty tonnage. The Abyssinia Crisis shows why the distinction matters: historically, nearly every available carrier became a potential front-line unit because their capabilities remained within reach of one another, whereas two much larger Admirals would make role specialization harder to ignore. Only Furious was fast enough to accompany the Admiral conversions directly, making replacement-aircraft support a more convincing use than asking her smaller air group to duplicate their strike role. Treaty totals would still force difficult choices, and Lexington and Saratoga's declared displacement of exactly the permitted 37,000 tons draws pointed scepticism.

evidence.note: The Abyssinia Crisis and carrier role overlap, support and cruiser-carrier assignments, treaty displacement accounting, and the possible early loss of Argus.

segments.summary: The alternate fleet assigns older and smaller carriers to support, training, cruiser, and regional duties around two large strike carriers.

segments.title: Argus and Queen Bee target drones
segments.body: Clarke calls Argus, carrying Queen Bee drones by 1939, the world's first drone carrier. The aircraft were used mainly as targets for anti-aircraft drills. The strike capability attributed to them is theoretical.

evidence.note: Argus's Queen Bee drones, principally used for anti-aircraft target practice, with a theoretical strike role mentioned.

segments.summary: Argus's Queen Bee aircraft put drone operations at sea decades before modern uncrewed carrier proposals.

segments.title: Large hangars and twin-engine carrier aircraft
segments.body: Large Admiral-class conversions might have carried tall single hangars resembling those of Lexington and Saratoga. Their capacity could exceed the practical ability to operate an air group of more than 100 aircraft, encouraging fewer, larger twin-engine strike aircraft or fighters. That approach would also suit the Royal Navy's desired operating ranges. Experience with those aircraft could change Ark Royal's later layout: one large hangar, or separate hangars with enough height for twin-engine aircraft above a lower fighter space. The alternative low fighter hangar is suggested at roughly 14 or 15 feet, rather than giving both hangars similar heights.

evidence.note: Large single hangars, limits on managing very large air groups, twin-engine aircraft, and alternative hangar arrangements for Ark Royal.

segments.summary: Large Admiral-class conversions could encourage twin-engine naval aircraft and alter the hangar layout of later carriers.

segments.title: A compact deck-edge lift for an enclosed hangar
segments.body: Deck-edge lifts could free internal space, but aircraft losses and violent weather in the North Sea made an exposed hangar opening unattractive. A compact American arrangement offered another possibility. Its small platform supported the aircraft's main wheels while a projecting runner carried the tail wheel, reducing the lift's overall structure. The example is initially recalled uncertainly and then identified as Wasp. A similar lift could sit outside the enclosed hangar, with substantial doors shutting off the opening when required. This remains a proposed adaptation within the Admiral-carrier scenario.

evidence.note: The compact Wasp lift's main-wheel platform and tail-wheel runner, North Sea concerns, and a proposed external lift behind substantial hangar doors.

segments.summary: A Wasp-style lift could free internal space while allowing heavy doors to close the hangar against North Sea weather.

segments.title: Blackburn Blackburn spotting and early warning
segments.body: The Blackburn Blackburn was designed to carry a full naval chart and spotting table for gunnery control. Its crew also used telescopes and binoculars to watch for approaching aircraft and radio warnings to the fleet. Those functions anticipate capabilities that later became essential to carrier operations. The aircraft's awkward appearance becomes a joke, but its spotting and warning roles explain why the design was useful.

evidence.note: The naval chart and spotting table, visual observation of approaching aircraft, and radio warnings.

segments.summary: The Blackburn Blackburn combined naval spotting equipment with visual warning of approaching aircraft.

segments.title: Three Admiral-class carriers before the Washington treaty
segments.body: The remaining Admiral-class battlecruisers were suspended in March 1917 and cancelled in February 1919. Clarke considers an alternative decision in 1918: restart all three as carrier conversions, either alongside Eagle or in its place. Britain would then approach the Washington negotiations with three large carrier conversions already under way. The treaty would have to account for that different programme, creating another route to a larger interwar carrier force.

evidence.note: The suspension and cancellation dates and Clarke's proposed 1918 conversion of all three hulls before the Washington negotiations.

segments.summary: Restarting all three suspended Admiral-class hulls as carriers would change the fleet Britain brought to the Washington negotiations.

segments.title: Strike, fleet, and cruiser carrier doctrine
segments.body: Cruiser carriers supported trade protection and cruiser operations; fleet carriers supplied reconnaissance, fighters, spotting, and some attack power; strike carriers delivered the major offensive blow. The strike-carrier lineage reached back to First World War schemes for attacking the High Seas Fleet in Wilhelmshaven, giving Ark Royal a specifically British ancestry. The Swordfish's torpedo-spotter-reconnaissance combination suited the fleet-carrier role. British doctrine also emphasised a continuing flow of smaller aircraft groups, although it retained the ability to assemble a larger strike. The roles came from the tasks assigned to each air group, with ship size following operational purpose.

evidence.note: Cruiser-, fleet- and strike-carrier roles, the Wilhelmshaven strike requirement, Swordfish duties, and smaller successive aircraft groups.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy distinguished strike-carrier, fleet-carrier, and cruiser-carrier concepts between the wars.

segments.title: Armored Ark Royals and multi-carrier operations
segments.body: The preferred late-interwar design resembles an Implacable-sized armoured Ark Royal, with enough aircraft for both fleet and strike roles and protection suited to distant theatres. The Far East requirement matters as much as the Mediterranean because a badly damaged carrier might have to return to Britain, while the RAF's reinforcement plan expected carriers to ferry land-based aircraft eastward. The treaty debate separates the maximum size of one carrier from Britain's total carrier tonnage. Experience operating Admiral conversions with roughly 100 aircraft might make larger individual carriers acceptable, because one ship could provide the air strength that historically required two smaller carriers. The Rear Admiral Aircraft Carriers appointment already provided command for multi-carrier operations. Taranto was intended as a two-carrier attack, but damage kept Eagle out and left Illustrious to conduct it alone. Larger, more survivable ships could make those established ambitions more attainable by reducing the number of carriers lost or sidelined.

evidence.note: Armoured Ark Royal concepts, Far East repair constraints, treaty tonnage choices and the Royal Navy's established multi-carrier ambitions.

segments.summary: The ideal late-interwar design combines Ark Royal's air group with armor, while larger surviving carriers make multi-carrier operations more attainable.

segments.title: Carrier armour and the Far East reinforcement problem
segments.body: A carrier badly damaged in Far Eastern operations would have to return to Britain for major repairs. Armour therefore addressed the risk of losing carrier support during a long voyage and refit, as well as surviving the immediate attack. The RAF's proposed reinforcement method was to unload the Fleet Air Arm, ferry RAF aircraft east and then send the carriers back for their naval aircraft. Those repeated transits left the Royal Navy without its normal carrier air groups while reinforcement was under way. Japanese operations would continue while the carriers shuttled between Britain and the Far East.

evidence.note: Far East repair distances and the RAF plan to ferry aircraft aboard carriers before returning for their naval air groups.

segments.summary: Far East deployment made repair distance a carrier-design problem, while the RAF reinforcement plan required the same ships to ferry aircraft east.

segments.title: Survivable fleet carriers and smaller ASW escorts
segments.body: Courageous was especially vulnerable because her large-light-cruiser origins provided neither the subdivision nor torpedo defense of an Admiral-class hull. A larger conversion might survive the U-boat attack that sank her, but that durability would not make submarine hunting a sensible use of such a valuable ship. A repeatable 10,000-ton Hermes-style cruiser carrier would instead handle convoy escort and anti-submarine work, leaving the fleet carriers for tasks that needed their speed and air groups. Under the early treaty definition, a ship below 10,000 tons did not count as a carrier, so a joking proposal declares a new design at 9,999 tons even though historical Hermes missed the threshold by about 500 tons. A series of such small carriers could also cover enough support work to make a separate Unicorn-style maintenance carrier less necessary. The Glorious scenario changes because a larger air group could carry rescued RAF aircraft without surrendering the ability to maintain a defensive patrol. With ample aircraft and a senior flag staff aboard, the absence of combat air patrol would be much harder to excuse.

evidence.note: Admiral-class protection compared with Courageous and Glorious, the treaty threshold for Hermes-type carriers and their potential support duties.

segments.summary: Replacing Courageous and Glorious with larger Admiral conversions changes both the damage the fleet carriers might survive and which ships should accept convoy and submarine-hunting risk.

segments.title: How a larger carrier could change the Glorious encounter
segments.body: In the counterfactual, an Admiral-class carrier has enough aircraft capacity to rescue RAF aircraft from Norway while retaining a useful naval air group. Its greater size also makes substantial flag staff facilities and an admiral aboard more likely. A senior commander would have fewer grounds to accept sailing without an aerial patrol when enough aircraft were available. An early sighting of the German battlecruisers could allow the carrier to turn away before contact. It might also launch torpedo aircraft and report the German ships to Warspite or Renown, making reconnaissance a major change alongside additional protection.

evidence.note: Additional aircraft capacity, flag staff oversight, aerial reconnaissance, avoidance and possible attacks in the alternate Glorious encounter.

segments.summary: A larger replacement for Glorious could rescue RAF aircraft while maintaining reconnaissance, giving it time to avoid or attack the German battlecruisers.

segments.title: Who paid for the interwar Fleet Air Arm?
segments.body: The Royal Navy financed the Fleet Air Arm while the Air Ministry administered its pilots through the RAF and controlled the procurement interface with manufacturers. Naval payments initially passed through the Air Ministry, which deducted administration costs before paying the aircraft companies. The change to direct naval payment is tentatively dated to around 1931, although the consistency of the arrangements remains unclear. Disputes arose when the Air Ministry accused the Navy of bypassing payment rules and the Navy questioned paying another department to deal with a firm such as Vickers that it already used.

evidence.note: Naval financing, Air Ministry administration fees and disputed direct payments to aircraft firms, with the policy change tentatively dated to about 1931.

segments.summary: The Navy financed the Fleet Air Arm even while the Air Ministry administered pilots, contracts, and the route to aircraft manufacturers.

segments.title: Why Malta and Midway converged
segments.body: Malta and Midway emerged from wartime lessons that brought British and American carrier design closer together. British enclosed armoured hangars restricted the ventilation needed to warm aircraft engines below deck, while American open hangars made that possible before aircraft reached the flight deck. American experience also showed that a large air group could be lost with the carrier's flying capability when a bomb or kamikaze ignited aircraft on an unarmoured flight deck. An armoured deck could preserve aircraft below and allow operations to resume after wreckage was cleared, even when aircraft parked above were lost. Both design traditions therefore moved toward an armoured flight deck and a hangar that could admit enough air for engine operation. Wartime experience also weakened the case for heavily armoured hangar sides: cruiser encounters were rare, and side armour would offer little protection once heavy gunfire caught the carrier.

evidence.note: British and American damage experience, warming engines in ventilated hangars and the reduced case for heavily armoured hangar sides.

segments.summary: British Malta and American Midway designs approached a common compromise between armored flight decks, large air groups, and ventilated hangars.

segments.title: Why operating areas shaped carrier armour and hangars
segments.body: Treaty limits had forced navies to trade air-group size against protection, and their removal gave British and American designers more freedom. The US Navy expected to operate across the wider Pacific, where sea room and air strength offered ways to avoid or disrupt attacks. British plans also required operations in the Mediterranean, the South China Sea and close to Japan, where limited manoeuvring room made protection more valuable. The Royal Navy's experience of North Sea conditions also complicated enthusiasm for a fully open hangar. A ventilated hangar needed enough airflow to warm engines without exposing the entire aircraft space as an open gallery.

evidence.note: Treaty freedom, operational geography and weather shaped the compromise between armour, air-group size and hangar ventilation.

segments.summary: Pacific sea room, confined British operating areas and North Sea weather produced different compromises between aircraft capacity, protection and hangar ventilation.

segments.title: False lessons from carrier exercises
segments.body: Exercise pilots often sought prestigious capital ships instead of attacking the first worthwhile target, while cruisers benefited from knowing the limited operating area in which a carrier had to be found. Real combat removed both assumptions: pilots facing lethal defenses might attack an exposed destroyer, and carriers could maneuver across a much larger sea area. Even very large exercises retain artificial limits because ships and aircrew must not actually be destroyed, so successful exercise behavior is not automatically sound wartime behavior. Exercises remain useful when analysts separate genuine operational insight from behavior created by safety rules and scenario boundaries.

evidence.note: Target incentives and bounded exercise areas could generate misleading results about air attacks and carrier interception.

segments.summary: Artificial exercise boundaries could exaggerate the ability of cruisers to find carriers and distort which ships attacking aircraft would choose.

segments.title: The Royal Navy's surviving postwar carrier fleet
segments.body: Britain entered the postwar period with several carrier classes whose different air-group sizes complicated logistics, training and combined operations. The proposed replacement programme begins by treating the worn Illustrious class as temporary training and reserve ships, with Illustrious herself preserved as a museum. Their low hangars and armoured box structure make major changes difficult, as Victorious's expensive reconstruction illustrates. The newer, larger Implacables retain enough machinery life to provide an interim operational force. Light carriers and the unfinished Audacious ships then support the transition toward the planned Malta class.

evidence.note: The surviving carrier fleet, its logistical variety and the proposed transition away from the worn Illustrious class.

segments.summary: Britain's crowded postwar carrier fleet included worn wartime ships and newer hulls worth developing for the jet age.
segments.question: What did the Royal Navy have as its surviving postwar carrier fleet before considering further construction?
segments.answerShort: The survivors included the Illustrious and Implacable classes, Unicorn and the elderly Furious and Argus, with Colossus and Majestic light carriers coming into service. The proposed plan retires the worn Illustrious class from front-line service and retains the Implacables temporarily.

segments.title: Why wartime carrier machinery wore out so quickly
segments.body: High-speed steaming aged carrier machinery even when the hull escaped serious battle damage. Repeated acceleration for flight operations made a carrier's duty cycle closer to a destroyer's than a battleship's. The rough comparison puts carrier wear near six peacetime years for each wartime year, leaving the Illustrious class with perhaps half a decade of useful steaming after 1945. Victorious's worn engines therefore fit the wartime operating pattern, and their condition had already prompted repeated reports before the reconstruction exposed how much work was needed.

evidence.note: Carrier and destroyer machinery wear compared with battleship use, including warnings about Victorious's engines.

segments.summary: Repeated high-speed flight operations gave aircraft carriers destroyer-like machinery wear, leaving the Illustrious class with little economical postwar life.

segments.title: Use light carriers to perfect the jet-age fleet
segments.body: The proposal deliberately slows Malta construction while accelerating two Audacious ships as conventional straight-deck carriers. Spreading expenditure over more years leaves room to rebuild the merchant fleet and address rationing while new carrier equipment is tested. This requires avoiding the historical Ark Royal mistake: she sat close to completion without being fully watertight, allowing weather exposure to degrade systems and burden her later service. Colossus and Majestic hulls become inexpensive test beds for steam catapults, angled decks, and other emerging systems rather than risking the operational Implacables. Once the configuration is proven, two more Audacious ships and four Maltas enter service with angled decks from the outset. This larger carrier program could also sustain completion of more Daring-class destroyers as its primary escorts. The experimental light carriers can then be sold abroad. The resulting force centers on four Malta-class and two angled-deck Audacious carriers, with the original two straight-deck Audacious ships available for support.

evidence.note: Staged construction, trials in light carriers, the resulting Audacious and Malta force and the need for Daring-class escorts.

segments.summary: A staged program uses light carriers for experiments before completing Audacious and Malta hulls with mature jet-age features.

segments.title: Build the Centaurs for amphibious assault and command
segments.body: The proposal completes roughly four Centaurs as amphibious assault and command ships. Their comparatively small hulls make an expensive conversion into angled-deck fleet carriers less attractive beside the larger Audacious and Malta classes. Completing them quickly avoids waiting for the full development of jet carrier arrangements. Catapults could be fitted but little used, or the ships could be prepared to receive them later. Helicopter operations give these ships a supporting role alongside the larger strike carriers and the straight-deck Audacious support ships.

evidence.note: Four Centaurs proposed for helicopter operations, amphibious assault and command, with optional or lightly used catapults.

segments.summary: The Centaur class becomes a purposefully limited helicopter, amphibious-assault, and command layer beneath the larger Audacious and Malta carrier force.

segments.title: Saving Ark Royal and Eagle for the Malta class
segments.body: The suggested programme would reserve Ark Royal, and perhaps Eagle, for Malta-class carriers larger than the Audacious ships. Africa is the proposed candidate for the Ark Royal name because renaming New Zealand would disregard a wartime ally's association with the programme. The historical Audacious programme already involved repeated renamings, with Audacious becoming Eagle and Irresistible becoming Ark Royal. Keeping those earlier names for the smaller ships would leave familiar carrier names available for the largest new hulls.

evidence.note: Africa considered for renaming as Ark Royal, New Zealand's wartime association and historical Audacious-class name changes.

segments.summary: The largest alternate carriers inherit the Royal Navy's most prestigious carrier names, with Africa treated as the Malta-class hull most easily renamed.

segments.title: Designing a carrier fleet to survive Treasury cuts
segments.body: The proposed fleet protects four Malta-class strike carriers by retaining older ships that can absorb successive budget cuts. Clarke initially favours retiring the straight-deck Audacious ships to preserve the Centaurs for the Royal Marines. Drachinifel prefers retiring all four Centaurs because that would remove four maintenance and training commitments and probably save more personnel than retiring two Audacious carriers. Under that approach, the straight-deck Audacious ships take over amphibious assault and command duties. The angled-deck pair can then fill the aircraft-support role, preserving a capability whose usefulness is illustrated by Unicorn's long postwar service. A later cut retires the straight-deck ships and moves the angled-deck carriers into helicopter assault work. This would reduce the fleet to six flight decks while retaining the Malta strike core, with fewer but more capable amphibious ships.

evidence.note: Clarke and Drachinifel's different retirement priorities, crew and maintenance savings, and successive transfers into aircraft-support and amphibious roles.

segments.summary: A layered fleet protects four Malta-class strike carriers by offering less capable ships for successive budget reductions.

segments.title: When the Malta carriers would need replacing
segments.body: By the late 1970s or early 1980s, the hypothetical Malta carriers would face worn hulls and machinery as well as increasingly large aircraft. Their useful lives would therefore require replacement planning even if successive budget cuts had spared the ships. Construction could begin in the early-to-mid 1980s, bringing new carriers into service around the end of that decade or the start of the 1990s. This timetable depends on the scenario preserving a substantial strike fleet through the defence cuts discussed here.

evidence.note: Projected Malta hull and machinery wear, aircraft growth, and an early-to-mid-1980s construction start for replacements.

segments.summary: Hull wear, machinery condition, and growing aircraft would put Malta replacements into construction in the early-to-mid 1980s.

segments.title: An Atlantic carrier navy as a diplomatic instrument
segments.body: A large British Atlantic carrier force could support a joint or alternating British-American strike command in this counterfactual. Regular carrier availability would also accustom governments to using a carrier group as a visible response to crises, making the force politically harder to cut. A heavier British Atlantic role would release American ships for the Pacific and other theatres. The proposed division would put British carriers in position to face the initial Soviet naval strikes, with American reinforcements arriving later. These are projected consequences of the alternate fleet, dependent on sustaining its strength and political support.

evidence.note: A proposed joint or alternating Atlantic strike command, carrier deployments as a diplomatic tool, and the hypothetical division of alliance responsibilities.

segments.summary: A sustained British carrier force could anchor NATO's Atlantic strike command and become a routine instrument of prime-ministerial signaling.

segments.title: How authoritarian institutions can preserve bad information
segments.body: Russian propaganda is criticised here for portraying Britain as both weak and decrepit and the powerful hidden enemy manipulating events. An anecdote about Chatham appearing in nuclear-target rhetoric leads to a second story about Soviet geography material identifying Edinburgh as the British capital. Dr Clarke recalls being told that this error affected the targeting of early missile silos, and reports finding support for the textbook claim. He explicitly has not checked the physical orientation of the silos and cannot verify that extension of the story. Fear of punishment for correcting or embarrassing a superior is offered as one reason an authoritarian institution could preserve a small factual error despite substantial technical capability.

evidence.note: Contradictory propaganda claims and the Edinburgh-capital anecdote, with Clarke's claimed textbook research distinguished from the unverified missile-silo story.

segments.summary: A caveated Soviet targeting story illustrates how propaganda, hierarchy, and fear can preserve factual errors inside a technically powerful state.

segments.title: A four-carrier replacement cycle for the 1980s
segments.body: Four identical replacement carriers could rotate between active strike duty, refit, hot standby, and Royal Marines helicopter support. Keeping catapults and the same basic hull configuration on all four would allow the helicopter carrier to embark Fleet Air Arm squadrons when a crisis required more strike capacity. Two carriers would already be at sea, with a third able to follow soon afterwards. Once the immediate need for several strike carriers passed, one could return to amphibious support, or the fourth could take that role after leaving refit. A hypothetical Falklands crisis tests this allocation: the stronger carrier force is expected to discourage an invasion, while Hawkeye support would reduce the number of carriers needed if fighting still occurred.

evidence.note: Four identical hulls rotating through strike, refit, standby, and helicopter support, with rapid air-group changes and a hypothetical Falklands deployment.

segments.summary: Four identical carriers could keep two hulls at sea and surge a third by changing the Royal Marines support ship's air group.

segments.title: A defensive carrier for reinforcing northern Norway
segments.body: A revised version of the replacement plan proposes four nuclear-powered carriers and considers how the Royal Marines would operate alongside them. Building Fearless-class landing ships with more helicopter capacity could spread amphibious aviation across the force and help justify a third LPD. Carrier protection would make reinforcement of northern Norway more secure and increase the usefulness of the landing force. The fourth carrier could carry a helicopter-heavy air group while retaining fighters and Hawkeyes for air defence. Its dedicated strike aircraft would move to the other carriers, preserving a distinction between defensive and strike air groups that still mattered in the 1980s.

evidence.note: A proposed nuclear carrier force, a possible third Fearless-class LPD, northern Norway reinforcement, and a helicopter-heavy fighter-and-Hawkeye air group.

segments.summary: A helicopter-heavy carrier with fighters and Hawkeyes could protect amphibious movement, while a larger Fearless force carried the Royal Marines.

segments.title: Would a navalized Tornado work?
segments.body: A carrier Tornado was physically possible, as the carrier-capable F-111B demonstrated for another large swing-wing aircraft. Short landing distances, an airbrake, and a parachute would not prepare Tornado's airframe for the loads of a carrier landing. Naval aircraft such as the Phantom and Buccaneer could transfer into land service with their structural strength already built in, while conversion in the other direction would require strengthening an established design. Very high-speed strike is conceded as a Tornado advantage over Buccaneer, but the difficult development of Tornado's air-defence version adds to the objections to creating a naval fighter variant. Viggen is suggested as a less difficult land-based starting point, although it would already be ageing by the 1980s.

evidence.note: Carrier-landing loads, the F-111B precedent, naval-to-land transfers, Tornado's limited strike advantage and air-defence development difficulties, and Viggen as an alternative.

segments.summary: A naval Tornado would need extensive structural redesign, while its strike and fighter roles offered little reason to accept the difficulty.
segments.question: How practical would a navalized Tornado have been, and would it have been better than the F-14 Tomcat?
segments.answerShort: It was physically possible, but the required airframe redesign and the limited advantages over existing naval aircraft made it an unattractive alternative to the F-14.

segments.title: A British fleet-defense fighter after Sea Vixen
segments.body: A larger Fleet Air Arm continuing through the 1960s and 1970s could support a British successor to Sea Vixen. That creates uncertainty about whether Phantom would enter service in this alternate fleet. If Phantoms still entered service, Malta-sized decks would remove the need for the Royal Navy's unusual extended nose gear and improve commonality. The P.1154 supersonic V/STOL concept offers another route to a fleet-defence fighter, especially if a larger naval order keeps the design effort alive. P.1127 is initially mentioned for the supersonic project, then corrected to P.1154. A later British role in the Super Hornet programme remains possible, depending on whether Britain ultimately buys American aircraft.

evidence.note: Alternative fighter procurement paths, reduced Phantom nose-gear requirements on larger decks, possible Super Hornet participation, and correction of the supersonic Harrier project's designation to P.1154.

segments.summary: Sustained naval aircraft orders could support a Sea Vixen successor, while larger decks simplify the alternative of operating Phantoms.

segments.title: An Anglo-French Super Jaguar for carrier strike
segments.body: Jaguar's rough-field design makes it a candidate for a carrier aircraft in this scenario. The historical Jaguar M provides a direct example of a naval strike variant, while the proposed Super Jaguar offers a possible later replacement for Buccaneer. Specifying carrier operation from the outset could produce an aircraft for British and French carriers that also served land-based squadrons. A hypothetical force of four British and two French carriers would improve the size of the shared market, although the number of French ships remains an open question. Britain operating roughly two-thirds of that carrier fleet would raise a dispute over how much money and work should go into the French side of the programme. Land-based aircraft able to operate from carriers could also reinforce naval squadrons when required.

evidence.note: Jaguar rough-field suitability, the Jaguar M precedent, a proposed carrier-capable Super Jaguar, hypothetical French carrier numbers, industrial workshare, and cross-deck use of land-based aircraft.

segments.summary: The proposed Super Jaguar turns an existing rough-field attack-aircraft family into a shared British and French carrier strike program.

segments.title: Use V/STOL fighters to launch air defense faster
segments.body: The proposed supersonic V/STOL fighter could operate alongside conventional aircraft on a large carrier. It might also use the flight decks of more helicopter-capable Fearless-class landing ships, even if it was not permanently based aboard them. On a fleet carrier, a rolling takeoff would let fighters launch without waiting for a catapult to reset. Fighters could use the angled deck or another suitable clear position while the catapults launched strike aircraft. This would allow a defensive fighter surge and a strike launch to proceed together.

evidence.note: Supersonic V/STOL fighters as a possible Phantom successor, operations from landing ships, and rolling fighter takeoffs alongside catapult-launched strikes.

segments.summary: Rolling takeoffs could get defensive fighters airborne while the carrier's catapults launched strike aircraft.

segments.title: Merchant ships as distributed fighter bases
segments.body: In the hypothetical Cold War fleet, large merchant ships could carry supersonic V/STOL fighters on simple landing pads with fuel and limited weapons support. A more elaborate containerised runway and hangar is considered, but a landing pad on a container ship or tanker is judged more realistic. These fighters would be difficult to integrate into the main carrier interception, so an air-defence destroyer within the convoy could control them as a local reserve. The fleet carrier could then commit its air wing against the main Backfire raid while the merchant-based fighters dealt with bombers or missiles that penetrated the outer defence. Common aircraft would allow fighters needing attention to return to the fleet carrier for servicing. The reserve would also provide some combat air patrol while the main force recovered after its interception.

evidence.note: Merchant landing-pad options, a destroyer-controlled local fighter reserve, compatibility with the fleet carrier, and protection while the main air wing recovered.

segments.summary: Supersonic V/STOL fighters could give merchant ships a limited self-defense role against Soviet bomber raids without creating full auxiliary carriers.

segments.title: A 1980s carrier fleet still serving with F-35s
segments.body: American experience with Enterprise and the Nimitz class shows that a large carrier can serve for roughly half a century. British replacements begun in the 1980s and commissioned around 1990 would therefore be only thirty to thirty-five years old in the scenario's present day. Their successors might not enter service until the mid-to-late 2030s, so planning could begin while the existing ships still had a decade or more of useful life. F-35Cs would suit the large catapult-equipped decks, while a mixed F-35B/F-35C air group would depend on whether earlier V/STOL fighters had proved useful for surging air defence during strike launches.

evidence.note: Projected carrier service into the 2030s and a conditional F-35B/F-35C mix based on the value of independent fighter launches.

segments.summary: In the video's present-day scenario, carriers commissioned around 1990 still have useful service ahead, with replacement planning and the F-35B/F-35C choice remaining open.

segments.title: Catapults and the cost of reducing carrier capacity
segments.body: Prolonging construction is criticised for leaving Britain with two carriers at roughly the cost of three. The preferred alternative fits catapults and F-35Cs from the beginning. Clarke still values the F-35B's vertical-takeoff capability, but agrees that the ships should have had catapults. Carrier dimensions also impose abrupt thresholds in aircraft capacity. A slightly wider hangar can make maintenance easier, whereas narrowing it by only a foot or two can remove an entire row of aircraft. Further reductions then save space without changing capacity until the next whole row becomes impossible to accommodate.

evidence.note: Construction delays, the preference for catapults and F-35Cs, the retained attraction of vertical takeoff, and whole-row thresholds in hangar capacity.

segments.summary: The preferred Queen Elizabeth design combines catapults and F-35Cs, while small reductions in hangar size can remove a large share of the air group.

segments.title: Would catapult-equipped Queen Elizabeth carriers need to be larger?
segments.body: Aircraft need enough hangar length and width to fit in complete rows and squadron-sized groups. The forward section of the existing Queen Elizabeth hangar is described as accommodating about half a squadron, with a modest extension potentially making room for a full one. Tentative figures put the folded F-35C at about 31 feet wide against the F-35B's 35-foot wingspan, despite the C reaching about 43 feet with its wings extended. A Hawkeye-type airborne early-warning aircraft would occupy more space than a Merlin helicopter, which also fits the anti-submarine role. Keeping such an aircraft on the flight deck is rejected because it would complicate maintenance. The design question therefore concerns the entire air group and its support needs, as well as the fighters.

evidence.note: Hangar length, provisional folded-aircraft dimensions, and the maintenance space needed for fixed-wing early-warning aircraft.

segments.summary: Hangar dimensions, folded fighters, and fixed-wing airborne early-warning aircraft determine whether a catapult-equipped carrier needs enlarging.
segments.question: Would Queen Elizabeth-class carriers need to be larger if they used catapults and operated F-35Cs?
segments.answerShort: A larger hangar is favoured, although folded F-35Cs would occupy less width than F-35Bs. Space for complete squadrons and fixed-wing airborne early-warning aircraft also matters.

segments.title: Why carriers endure when their aircraft change
segments.body: A battleship's combat value was tied closely to the weapons and protection built into its hull. A carrier supports naval aircraft whose weapons and capabilities can change during the ship's service life. Aircraft still need maintenance, weapons, fuel, and a place to recover, while their pilots need rest even when aerial refuelling extends their range. The carrier remains useful for as long as naval aviation needs that movable support base at sea.

evidence.note: Changing aircraft capabilities and the continuing need for maintenance, rearming, recovery, and pilot rest.

segments.summary: A carrier's striking power can change with its aircraft while the ship continues to provide the mobile base those aircraft need.

segments.title: How dockyards and bases shape carrier design
segments.body: The Queen Elizabeth design was fitted to the chosen Rosyth assembly site and its exit route. Dock gates constrained the beam, while passage beneath the Forth Bridge affected the masts. These restrictions embedded the choice of construction site in the ship's dimensions and added design work and cost. The French comparison attributes Charles de Gaulle's size constraints to political objections to using a particular yard, with subsequent government ownership opening that facility to a larger successor. Earlier British capital ships faced similar compromises: the Admiral class and G3 designs were constrained by the facilities available to build and handle them. Enlarging infrastructure and restricting the ship to existing facilities therefore produce different naval capabilities.

evidence.note: Rosyth's dock gates and the Forth Bridge constrained the Queen Elizabeth design, with comparable infrastructure restrictions on Charles de Gaulle and earlier British capital ships.

segments.summary: Construction docks, gates, and bridges can determine carrier dimensions before the desired air group has been fully accommodated.

segments.title: A second carrier base on Merseyside
segments.body: A larger carrier fleet raises the question of where Britain could establish a second base alongside Portsmouth. Merseyside is proposed because it has the water space and depth needed to bring large carriers in. Portsmouth's established naval role would still encourage investment in access and dredging. A Merseyside base would extend naval employment into another group of constituencies and give their MPs a direct interest in retaining the fleet. Cuts large enough to threaten the base would consequently create local political opposition as well as an operational loss.

evidence.note: Merseyside's suitability for large carriers and the constituency interests created by a second carrier base.

segments.summary: A larger carrier fleet could create a Merseyside base whose employment and local political support would help protect carrier numbers.

segments.title: Using ship names to protect a carrier program
segments.body: The proposal adapts a Royal Navy technique associated here with Town-class cruisers: attach major warships to places whose elected representatives will resist losing them. Capital-city names would distribute the political stakes across England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland. The modern Type 26 naming sequence provides a comparable example, especially when construction jobs and a prominent local ship name reinforce each other. The Royal Canadian Navy's River-class destroyer names - Fraser, St. Lawrence, and Mackenzie - offer a parallel by tying a major program to rivers crossing politically important regions. A local name may attract little attention while the program is safe, but cancellation can be reframed as a direct insult to the city or nation. The symbolism then becomes practical protection for the procurement program.

evidence.note: Capital-city carrier names, the Town-class precedent, Type 26 city names, and Canadian River-class names as protection against cancellation.

segments.summary: Naming four carriers London, Cardiff, Edinburgh, and Belfast would make cancellations politically costly across the United Kingdom.

segments.title: Project Ark Royal and a mixed carrier air group
segments.body: At the time of recording, Project Ark Royal was a study of possible conversion. Funding decisions, changes in senior naval leadership, and world events could redirect it before implementation. A prolonged period of mixed crewed and uncrewed air groups is expected. Drones could serve as loyal wingmen, tankers, or other support aircraft, or take the principal strike role while crewed fighters concentrate on air defence. Their place in the air group depends partly on whether they are treated as supporting aircraft or equivalent combat assets.

evidence.note: Project Ark Royal's study status and the possible division of missions between crewed aircraft and drones.

segments.summary: Project Ark Royal leaves open how crewed aircraft and drones would divide carrier missions and whether drones would be supporting aircraft or equivalent combat assets.

segments.title: Autonomous evasion and the next carrier drones
segments.body: Drachinifel points to recent reports of Russian reconnaissance drones using rear-facing sensors to detect approaching threats and begin programmed evasive manoeuvres. The sensor type remains uncertain: lidar, radar, and cameras are offered as possibilities. A remotely controlled aircraft can be vulnerable when its operator is watching the target area and never sees a missile approaching from elsewhere. Autonomous detection and evasion could reduce that dependence on the operator's field of view, including under heavy jamming. Technology small enough for expendable reconnaissance drones could also be applied to larger aircraft. The resulting carrier drones might gain substantial defensive and offensive autonomy sooner than expected, bypassing an intermediate generation mainly carrying extra weapons for crewed fighters.

evidence.note: Drachinifel's account of reported rear-facing drone sensors, their uncertain type, the limitations of remote observation, and possible implications for larger autonomous aircraft.

segments.summary: Small reconnaissance drones in Ukraine suggest how autonomous threat detection and evasive manoeuvres could improve the survivability of larger uncrewed aircraft.

segments.title: Drone-carrying drones and the old bomber problem
segments.body: Very small drones are judged a greater concern in confined waters, such as the Strait of Hormuz or Suez Canal, than for a carrier operating roughly a hundred miles offshore. Larger drones could reach farther, but their greater cost would make missile interception a more worthwhile exchange. A cheap carrier drone could alter that calculation by transporting many smaller autonomous drones to the edge of the defended area. It could release them at a programmed point or when a warning receiver detected a threat. The tactical problem resembles defence against Soviet Backfire bombers: intercept the delivery aircraft before it releases numerous smaller threats. Distance, the Earth's curvature, logistics, and the need to stop weapons that pass the outer defences would still constrain the defender.

evidence.note: Small-drone range limits, the economics of engaging larger drones, and a proposed drone carrier that recreates the problem of intercepting bombers before weapon release.

segments.summary: A cheap long-range drone could deliver many smaller autonomous drones, recreating the Cold War requirement to destroy bombers before weapon release.

segments.title: CV(A)-01 and the cost of abandoning a distinctive NATO role
segments.body: CV(A)-01 sought much of the capability the proposed Malta-centred programme would have established decades earlier, when more money and political room were available. The defence settlement prioritised Britain's place on NATO's central European front and put the services into competition for funding. Clarke's criticism is that this emphasis sacrificed maritime capabilities that made Britain a distinctive contributor to the alliance. In his view, another medium-sized army contribution offered less than retaining the alliance's second-largest navy, particularly when American reinforcement depended on crossing the Atlantic.

evidence.note: The alternate programme's effect on the need for CV(A)-01 and Clarke's criticism of prioritising the NATO central front over maritime reinforcement.

segments.summary: The alternate carrier programme bypasses CV(A)-01 and frames the central-front defence settlement as a loss of Britain's distinctive maritime contribution to NATO.

segments.title: When refits move a battlecruiser toward a fast battleship
segments.body: Dr Clarke places warships on a spectrum defined partly by armour coverage, subdivision, and hull density. He argues that additional subdivision introduced into at least two Kongo-class ships during their 1930s reconstructions moved them into fast-battleship territory. Drachinifel continues to classify them as battlecruisers. Their disagreement concerns how much the rebuilt ship's physical characteristics should change the classification inherited from its original design.

evidence.note: Clarke's subdivision-based argument for reclassifying at least two rebuilt Kongo-class ships and Drachinifel's continued use of the battlecruiser label.

segments.summary: The Kongo-class aside shows why warship classification can change as reconstruction alters protection, subdivision, and hull characteristics.

segments.title: Carrier hangars, naval diplomacy, and escalation
segments.body: Judging a warship only by its original design misses changes made during its service life, while judging it only by combat performance overlooks much of its peacetime work. Staterooms, entertaining facilities, and suitable deck space can contribute to naval diplomacy. Large carrier hangars can host receptions among imposing aircraft, turning aviation facilities into a setting for political influence. Before the Second World War, Britain could escalate a naval presence from routine sloop visits through cruisers, squadrons, and battleships. The Cold War compressed that range of options, leaving fewer levels of escalation before conflict. A fleet containing both Audacious- and Malta-sized carriers would offer a choice over the scale and meaning of a deployment before committing to combat.

evidence.note: Evaluating ships across refits and peacetime service, the diplomatic use of carrier spaces, and the graded naval presence available to a more varied fleet.

segments.summary: Carrier hangars support diplomacy as well as aircraft, while a varied fleet gives governments more rungs on the ladder between routine presence and combat.
